cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK IX
"I am Odysseus": the Cicones, the Lotus-eaters, and the Cyclops.
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Lord Alcinous, most renowned among all peoples,\ntruly it is a fine thing to hear a singer
such as this man is, with a voice like the gods'.
For I say there is no accomplishment more\ngraceful than when joy holds a whole people,
and feasters up and down the\nhall sit listening to a singer,
seated in order, and beside them the tables are loaded\nwith bread and meats, and the cupbearer draws wine
from the bowl and carries it round and fills the cups:
this seems to my mind the fairest thing there is.
But your heart has turned to asking after my grievous\ncares — so that I may mourn and groan the more.
What first, then, what last shall I tell through?
For the gods of heaven have\ngiven me sorrows past counting.
Now first I will tell my name, so that you too may know it —\nand I hereafter, if I escape the pitiless day,
may be your guest-friend, though my home is far away.
I am Odysseus, son of Laertes — known to all mankind\nfor my cunning designs; and my fame has reached heaven.
My home is Ithaca, clear-skied under its mountain,
Neriton, tall in its shivering leaves; and around\nit islands lie in a cluster, close to one another —
Dulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus.
Ithaca itself lies low, farthest out in the sea toward\nthe dark of sunset — the rest face dawn and the sun —
rough ground, but a good nurse of men. I cannot
see any sweeter sight, for my part,\nthan a man's own country.
The queenly goddess Calypso would\nhave kept me there beside her
in her hollow caves, hungry to make me her husband,\nand so, in the same way, Circe detained me in her halls,
the guileful lady of Aeaea, hungry to make me her husband:
but they never once persuaded the heart in my breast.
So true it is that nothing is\nsweeter than a man's own country
and his own parents, even if he lives in a rich house\nfar away in a strange land, cut off from his parents.
But come — let me tell you also my\njourney home, and all its cares,
which Zeus laid on me on the way from Troy.
From Ilium the wind bore me to the Cicones — to Ismarus.\nThere I sacked the city and destroyed the men;
and out of the city we took their wives and much substance
and divided all, so that no man\nmight go cheated of his share by me.
Then, you may be sure, I ordered a quick-footed retreat —\nand they, the great fools, would not obey.
There and then much wine was being drunk, and many sheep
they slaughtered along the shore,\nand shambling crook-horned cattle;
and meanwhile Cicones went crying to Cicones,\ntheir neighbors inland — more of them, and better men,
skilled at fighting men from chariots and,\nwhere need was, on foot.
They came, then, thick as leaves\nand flowers come in their season,
in the morning mist. Then an evil doom of Zeus stood by us,\nluckless men, to load us with pains in plenty.
They set their battle-line and fought by the fast ships,
and each side pelted each with bronze-tipped spears.
As long as it was morning,\nand the sacred day still growing,
so long we stood them off and held\nour ground, though they were more;
but when the sun turned over toward unyoking-time,\nthen the Cicones broke the Achaeans, and mastered them.
Six from each ship, six strong-greaved companions\nwere killed; the rest of us fled from death and doom.
From there we sailed on further, grieved at heart,\nglad to be out of death, having lost our dear companions.
But my curved ships would not go forward before we had\ncalled three times on each of those poor companions
who died on the plain, cut down by the Cicones.
And Zeus who gathers the clouds roused\nthe North Wind against the ships
in a howling squall, and covered land and sea\nalike with cloud; and night rose up out of heaven.
The ships were swept along slantwise, their sails
ripped into three and four rags\nby the strength of the wind.
We lowered them into the hulls, in terror of death,\nand rowed the ships hard in toward the shore.
There for two nights and two days without a break
we lay, eating our hearts with\nweariness and pain together.
But when Dawn of the lovely braids\nbrought the third day round,
we set up the masts and hauled the white sails open
and sat, and the wind and the\nsteersmen held them on course.
And now I would have come unharmed to my own country,\nbut the wave and the current, as I rounded Malea,
and the North Wind beat me off\ncourse and drove me wide of Cythera.
From there for nine days I was carried by ruinous winds
across the fish-filled sea;\nand on the tenth we stepped ashore
in the land of the Lotus-eaters,\nwho eat a flower for food.
There we set foot on the mainland and drew water,
and the companions quickly took\ntheir meal beside the fast ships.
And when we had tasted food and drink,\nthen I sent companions ahead to learn
what men they were who ate bread upon this earth:
two men I chose, and sent a third with them as herald.
They went their way at once,\nand fell in with the Lotus-eater men;
and the Lotus-eaters had no thought of killing our\ncompanions — but they gave them lotus to taste.
And whoever of them ate the honey-sweet fruit of the\nlotus no longer wished to bring back word or to return:
there they wanted to stay, among the Lotus-eater men,\nbrowsing the lotus, and to forget their homecoming.
These men I forced back weeping to the ships,
dragged them under the benches of\nthe hollow ships and bound them,
and I ordered the rest of my trusted\ncompanions to hurry and board the fast ships —
for fear some other might eat of\nthe lotus and forget his homecoming.
And they came aboard at once and\ntook their places at the oarlocks,
and sitting in order they struck\nthe gray salt water with their oars.
From there we sailed on further, grieved at heart.
And we came to the land of the Cyclopes — the overweening,
the lawless — who, trusting in the deathless gods,\nplant no crop with their hands, and plow nothing:
everything springs up for them unsown,\nunplowed, wheat and barley, and vines that carry
wine in their heavy clusters,\nand Zeus' rain swells it for them.
They have no counsel-bearing assemblies, no established laws,\nbut live on the crests of the high mountains
in hollow caves, and each man lays down the law
to his own wives and children —\nand they care nothing for one another.
Now a scrubby island stretches outside the harbor there,\nneither close in to the Cyclopes' land nor far out,
wooded; and on it goats past counting breed,\nwild goats: no tread of men scares them away,
no hunters push through to it, men who suffer hard\ndays in the timber, working the mountain crests;
it is held by no flocks and no plowed fields,\nbut unsown and unplowed all its days
the island is widowed of men,\nand feeds its bleating goats.
For the Cyclopes have no red-cheeked ships,\nand no shipwrights among them who might labor out
well-benched vessels to accomplish every need,\ncrossing to the cities of the world, the way men
so often traverse the sea in ships to one another:
such craftsmen would have made\nthe island a fair settlement too.
For it is not a bad island at all:\nit would bear every crop in season.
There are meadows in it along the\nshores of the gray salt water,
soft, well-watered; vines there would never die;\nthere is level plowland, and a deep standing harvest always
ready for the scythe in season,\nfor the soil beneath is rich.
And there is a harbor with safe anchorage,\nwhere there is no need of mooring-line —
no anchor-stones to throw, no stern-cables to make fast:
you beach her, and wait until the sailors'\nhearts prompt them, and the breezes blow.
And at the harbor's head runs shining water,\na spring under a cave, with black poplars growing round it.
There we sailed in — and some god was guiding us —\nthrough the dead of night, with nothing to be seen ahead:
a fog lay thick around the ships, and the moon\nshowed nothing from heaven, shut in by clouds.
No one's eyes made out that island then, nor did we\nsee the long combers rolling in against the shore
before the well-benched ships ran up the beach.
And with the ships beached, we took down all the sails
and stepped out ourselves onto the surf-line of the sea,
and there we dropped asleep, and waited for shining Dawn.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,\nwe walked that island marveling, all through it.
And the nymphs, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus, started
the mountain goats,\nso my companions might have their meal.
At once we fetched our curved\nbows and long-socketed goat-spears
out of the ships, and forming in three bands
we shot; and quickly the god gave\nus game to our hearts' content.
Twelve ships followed with me, and to each nine\ngoats fell by lot; for me alone they picked out ten.
So then all day long till the setting of the sun we\nsat feasting on meat past counting and sweet wine.
For the red wine was not from out our ships:
there was still some left,\nfor each crew had drawn off much
in two-handled jars when we\ntook the Cicones' holy citadel.
And we looked across at the land\nof the Cyclopes, who were near:
smoke, and voices — theirs, and their sheep's and goats'.
And when the sun went down and the dusk came on,\nthen we lay down to sleep on the surf-line of the sea.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,
then I called an assembly, and spoke among them all:
'The rest of you stay here now, my trusted companions,\nwhile I with my own ship and my own crew
go and make trial of those men over there — what they are:
whether violent, savage, without justice,\nor kind to strangers, with hearts that fear the gods.'
So speaking I went aboard, and ordered my companions\nto board in their turn and loose the stern-cables.
And they came aboard at once and\ntook their places at the oarlocks,
and sitting in order they struck\nthe gray salt water with their oars.
But when we reached the place — it was not far —\nthere on the land's edge, close by the sea, we saw a cave,
high, overhung with laurels. There many flocks —\nsheep and goats — were penned at night; around it a yard
ran high-built, of stones set deep in the earth,\nand tall pines, and oaks with lofty crowns.
And there a man slept, a monster of a man, who shepherded\nhis flocks alone and far apart; he kept no company
with others, but held aloof, and his heart knew no law.
For he was built a monstrous wonder — nothing\nlike a man who eats bread, but like a wooded crag
of the high mountains, standing clear of all the rest.
Then I ordered the rest of my trusted companions\nto stay there by the ship and guard the ship,
while I picked the twelve best of my companions\nand went. And I took a goatskin of dark wine,
sweet wine, that Maron gave me, Euanthes' son,\nthe priest of Apollo, the god who watches over Ismarus —
because we had protected him, with his child and his wife,
out of reverence: for he lived in the wooded grove\nof Phoebus Apollo. And he gave me shining gifts:
he gave me seven talents of well-wrought gold,\nand he gave me a mixing-bowl all of silver, and then
wine, drawn off in two-handled jars, twelve in all,\nsweet and unmixed, a drink for gods. Not one
of the slaves or handmaids in his house knew of it —
only himself and his dear wife, and one housekeeper only.
Whenever they drank that honey-sweet red wine,\nhe would fill one cup and pour it into twenty measures
of water, and a sweet smell would rise from the bowl,\na marvel: no joy then in holding back.
Of this I filled a great skin and\nbrought it, and provisions too
in a sack: for my proud heart had a foreboding, even then,
that a man would come against\nme clothed in great strength,
a savage, knowing nothing of judgments or of laws.
Quickly we came to the cave, and did not find him within:\nhe was herding his fat flocks in the pasture.
We went into the cave and stared in wonder at everything:
crates sagging with cheeses; pens crowded with\nlambs and kids — each sort folded separately,
the firstlings apart, apart the middle-born,\napart again the newborn; and every vessel swimming with whey,
the pails and bowls, all made\nby hand, that he milked into.
There first my companions begged me, pleading:
take some cheeses and go back; then quickly,\ndriving the kids and lambs out of their pens
down to the fast ship, sail away over the salt water.
But I would not listen — it would have been far better —
not until I saw him, and whether\nhe would give me guest-gifts.
And his appearing was to be no joy to my companions.
We lit a fire there and made an\noffering, and helped ourselves
to cheeses, and ate, and sat inside waiting for him,\nuntil he came back herding. He carried a huge weight
of dry wood, to serve him at supper-time,\nand flung it down inside the cave with a crash;
and we in terror shrank away into the cave's far corner.
He drove his fat flocks into the wide cavern —\nall those he milked; the males he left outside,
the rams and he-goats, out in the deep yard.
Then he lifted high and set in place a huge door-stone,\na massive thing: twenty-two carts, good ones,
four-wheeled, could not have levered it off the ground —
such a towering cliff of rock he set in the doorway.
Then, sitting, he milked the ewes and bleating goats,\nall in due order, and set the young under each.
And straightway he curdled half the white milk and\ngathered it and stored it in the plaited baskets,
and half he stood in vessels, so it might be there for\nhim to take and drink, and serve him at supper-time.
And when at last he had hurried through his work,\nthen he lit the fire — and saw us, and asked:
'Strangers, who are you?\nFrom where do you sail the watery ways?
Is it on some business — or do you rove at\nrandom, the way sea-raiders do, who wander
staking their own lives, bearing evil to strangers?'
So he spoke, and our own hearts broke within us in\nterror of the deep voice and the monster himself.
Even so I answered him, and said:
'We are Achaeans, blown off course from Troy by every\nwind there is, across the great gulf of the sea,
making for home — but by other routes, other roads\nwe came: so Zeus, I suppose, chose to devise it.
We declare ourselves the people of Agamemnon, Atreus' son,
whose fame is now the greatest thing under heaven,\nso vast the city he sacked, so many the peoples
he destroyed. But we, for our part,\nhave come to your knees
in hope you may offer guest-friendship — or give besides
some gift, as is the right and custom done for strangers.
Respect the gods, mighty one. We are your suppliants,
and Zeus is the avenger of suppliants and of strangers —
Zeus of Strangers, who walks beside honored guests.'
So I spoke, and he answered me\nat once, with pitiless heart:
'You are a fool, stranger —\nor you have come from far away —
you who tell me to fear the gods or shun their anger.
The Cyclopes pay no heed to Zeus who bears the aegis,
nor to the blessed gods: for we are the better men by far.
I would not spare you or your companions to dodge\nthe hatred of Zeus — not unless my own heart bade me.
But tell me: where did you moor\nyour well-made ship when you came?
At the far end of the shore, or near? I want to know.'
So he spoke, testing; but I knew too much, and he did\nnot catch me; I answered him back with words of guile:
'My ship — Poseidon the\nearth-shaker smashed her to pieces,
driving her on the rocks at the border of your country:
and the wind carried her in from the sea.
But I, with these men here, escaped sheer destruction.'
So I spoke; and out of his\npitiless heart he answered nothing,
but sprang up and reached his hands out at my companions,
snatched up two together, and dashed them like puppies
against the ground: their brains\nran out on the earth, and wetted it.
He tore them limb from limb and made ready his supper,
and he ate like a mountain-bred lion, and left nothing —
the entrails, the flesh, the bones with their marrow.
And we, weeping, lifted up our hands to Zeus at the\nhorror we watched, helplessness holding our hearts.
And when the Cyclops had filled his great belly,\nfeeding on man-flesh and washing it down with unmixed milk,
he lay stretched out in the cave among his sheep.
And I made a plan in my own great heart to steal close,\ndraw the sharp sword from beside my thigh,
and stab him in the chest,\nwhere the midriff holds the liver,
feeling for the place with my hand.\nBut a second thought held me:
there we too would have perished in sheer destruction,\nfor we could never have pushed back with our hands
the massive stone he had set in the high doorway.
So then, groaning, we waited for shining Dawn.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,
then he lit the fire, and milked his famous flocks,\nall in due order, and set the young under each.
And when at last he had hurried through his work,
he snatched up two men together\nagain, and made his meal ready.
And having fed, he drove his fat flocks out of the cave,
lifting off the great door-stone with ease — and then\nset it back, the way a man sets the lid on a quiver.
With a great whistling the Cyclops turned his fat flocks
toward the mountain; and I was left\nbrooding evil deep in my heart:
if somehow I might pay him back,\nand Athena grant me the glory.
And this, as I turned it over, seemed to me the best plan.
There lay beside a pen a great club of the Cyclops',\ngreen olive-wood: he had cut it to carry
once it seasoned. Looking it over we judged it\nbig as the mast of a black twenty-oared ship,
a broad-beamed freighter, that crosses the great gulf:
that was its length, that its thickness to the eye.
Standing to it, I cut off about a fathom's measure
and handed it to my companions,\nand told them to dress it down;
and they made it smooth,\nwhile standing by I brought it to a point
at the tip, and then took it and\nhardened it in the blazing fire.
And I laid it carefully by, hiding it under the dung
that was strewn in a great deep litter through the cave.
And I told the others to shake lots among them for\nwho would dare, together with me, to lift the stake
and grind it in his eye, when sweet sleep came on him.
The lot fell on the very men I would have chosen —
four of them, and I counted\nmyself in with them, the fifth.
At evening he came back, herding his fair-fleeced flocks,
and drove those fat flocks straight into the wide cavern,
all of them: he left not one outside in the deep yard,
whether some foreboding moved him, or a god so ordered it.
Then he lifted high and set in place the great door-stone,
and sitting, he milked the ewes and bleating goats,\nall in due order, and set the young under each.
And when at last he had hurried through his work,
he snatched up two men together again,\nand made his supper ready.
And then I came up close and spoke to the Cyclops,\nholding in my hands an ivy-wood bowl of the dark wine:
'Cyclops — here, drink wine,\nnow you have fed on man-flesh:
so you may know what kind of drink our ship
carried stored. I was bringing it\nas an offering for you, in hope
you might pity me and send me home.\nBut your madness is past all bearing.
Merciless one — how will any other man of all the many
ever come near you again?\nWhat you have done is past all measure.'
So I spoke; and he took it, and drank it down;\nand it pleased him — terribly —
the sweet drink; and he demanded a second helping:
'Give me more — be generous. And tell me your name,
here, now, so I can give you a\nguest-gift that will make you glad.
The grain-giving plowland bears\nwine for the Cyclopes too —
fine clusters, and Zeus' rain swells them for us;\nbut this — this is a rivulet of ambrosia and nectar!'
So he spoke, and I handed him the fire-bright wine again.
Three times I brought and gave it;\nthree times, in his folly, he drained it.
And when the wine had come circling round the Cyclops' wits,\nthen I spoke to him with honeyed words:
'Cyclops, you ask my glorious name? Then I will tell it —\nand you give me the guest-gift, as you promised.
Nobody is my name. Nobody is what they call me —\nmy mother and my father and all my companions.'
So I spoke, and he answered me\nat once, with pitiless heart:
'Nobody I will eat last of all his company,\nand the others before him. That shall be your guest-gift.'
He spoke — and reeling back he fell flat, and lay there\nwith his thick neck lolled over sideways; and sleep
the all-subduer took him. And from his gullet gushed wine
and gobbets of human flesh,\nas he belched in his drunkenness.
And then I drove the stake under the deep ash-heap\nto heat; and with my words I put courage in all
my companions, so no man might flinch and hang back.
But when that olive stake in\nthe fire, green though it was,
was on the point of catching,\nand glowed clean through, terrible —
then I brought it close out of the fire, and my companions
stood round me; and a great\npower breathed courage into us.
They took up the olive stake, sharpened at its point,
and rammed it in his eye; and I,\nthrowing my weight on from above,
spun it — the way a man bores a ship-timber with\na drill, and his mates below keep it running
with a strap they hold at either end,\nand it spins on without stopping:
so we took the fire-pointed stake and spun it in his eye,\nand the blood came boiling up round its heat,
and the blast singed all his lids and brows away
as the eyeball burned, and the\nroots of it crackled in the fire.
As when a smith dips a great axe-head or an\nadze in cold water, and it hisses loud and high,
tempering it — for that is what gives iron its strength —\nso his eye hissed round the olive stake.
And he let out a huge and hideous howl,\nand the rock rang round it,
and we shrank back in terror. He wrenched the stake\nout of his eye, all fouled with streaming blood,
and flung it from him, flailing his arms in agony,\nand set up a great bellowing to the Cyclopes who lived
around him in caves along the windy heights.
And they heard his cry and came thronging from every side,
and standing round the cave they asked him what was wrong:
'What in the world, Polyphemus?\nWhat hurt, that you cry out so
through the ambrosial night and make us sleepless?
Surely no mortal is driving off\nyour flocks against your will?
Surely no one is killing you — by cunning or by force?'
And out of the cave strong Polyphemus answered them:
'Friends — Nobody is killing me,\nby cunning and not by force!'
And they answered with winged words, and gave it back:
'If nobody is forcing you, then — alone as you are —
it must be sickness from great Zeus,\nand there is no escaping that.
Pray to our father, the lord Poseidon.'
So they spoke as they went; and my own heart laughed,
how my name had utterly deceived him —\nthe name, and the flawless cunning.
But the Cyclops, groaning and heaving in his agonies,
groped with his hands and lifted\nthe stone from the doorway,
and sat himself down in the door with both arms spread,
in hope of catching anyone who\ntried to slip out with the sheep:
such a fool, I suppose, he hoped to find in me.
But I was planning how it might all come out best —
if I could find some release from death for my companions\nand for myself; and I wove every guile and design,
as a man does for his very life:\nfor the great evil was close.
And this, as I turned it over, seemed to me the best plan.
There were rams there, well-fed, thick in the fleece,\nfine big animals, their wool dark as violets.
These, working quietly, I lashed\ntogether with plaited withies —
the ones that monster slept on, the outlaw — in threes:
the middle one of each three carried a man, and the\nother two walked either side, protecting my companions.
So three sheep to each man. But for myself —\nthere was one ram, far the finest of all the flock;
I caught him along the back and\ncurled under his shaggy belly
and lay there; and in that wondrous fleece, with my\nhands twisted fast, I hung on, with an enduring heart.
So then, groaning, we waited for shining Dawn.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,\nthen the male flocks poured out toward pasture,
and the unmilked females bleated about the pens with\ntheir udders bursting. And their lord, worn down
by evil agonies, ran his hands\nalong the backs of all his sheep
as they stood up straight — and never sensed it, the fool:
my men bound under the breasts of his own fleecy sheep.
Last of the flock the great ram walked toward the doorway,
heavy with his wool — and with me,\nand my crowding thoughts.
And strong Polyphemus, running his hands over him, said:
'Old sweetheart — my ram — why last of all the flock
through the cave this time? Before,\nyou were never one to lag behind:
first, always first, striding out to graze the soft\nflowering grass, first to reach the running rivers,
first in your longing to turn home to the fold at\nevening. And now — last of all. Grieving, are you,
for your master's eye, that a coward of a man put out,
with his miserable companions,\nwhen he had crushed my wits with wine —
Nobody — who is not yet, I promise, clear of destruction.
If only you could think with me, if only you had a\nvoice to say where that man is dodging from my fury:
then his brains would be dashed\nagainst the floor and spattered
this way and that through the cave,\nand my heart would find
some ease from the evils this\nworthless Nobody has brought me.'
So speaking he sent the ram away from him, out the door.
And when we had gone a little\nway from the cave and the yard,
first I loosed myself from under the ram,\nand then set my companions free.
Swiftly then we drove those\nlong-shanked sheep, deep in fat,
turning again and again to look behind, until we came
to the ship. And a welcome sight\nwe were to our dear companions —
we who had escaped death —\nbut the others they wept and wailed for.
I would not have it: I frowned each man's tears back
and ordered them quickly to fling the fine-fleeced sheep
aboard in numbers, and sail out over the salt water.
And they came aboard at once and\ntook their places at the oarlocks,
and sitting in order they struck\nthe gray salt water with their oars.
But when I was as far offshore as a man's shout carries,\nthen I called to the Cyclops with jeering words:
'Cyclops! Not so weak a man's companions, after all,
were those you meant to eat by\nmain force in your hollow cave.
And your own evil deeds were bound to find you out —
merciless one — you who did not shrink from eating guests
in your own house. For that Zeus\nhas paid you, and the other gods.'
So I spoke, and the anger in his heart grew fiercer,
and he tore off the peak of a\ngreat mountain and hurled it,
and brought it down just ahead of the dark-blue prow —\nbarely — it missed the tip of the steering-oar;
and the sea heaved up under the falling rock, and the\nbackwash carried the ship straight in toward the land,
a flood-surge out of the deep,\nand drove her toward the shore.
But I seized a long pole in my hands and shoved\nher off and out, and roused my companions,
ordering them to fall to their\noars and get us clear of the evil,
nodding hard with my head; and they bent to it and rowed.
But when we were twice as far out over the sea,
then I made to call to the Cyclops\nagain; and around me my companions
tried to hold me back with honeyed\nwords, this one and that one:
'Merciless man — why must you provoke a savage
who even now, with that shot\ninto the sea, has driven the ship
straight back ashore — and we thought we died there!
If he had heard a voice, heard any one of us speaking,
he would have smashed our heads\nand the ship's timbers together
with one jagged boulder: he throws that far.'
So they spoke, but they could not persuade my great heart,\nand I called back to him with fury in my breast:
'Cyclops — if any mortal man ever asks you\nwho put the shameful blinding on your eye,
tell him: Odysseus, sacker of cities, blinded me —\nthe son of Laertes, who has his home in Ithaca.'
So I spoke, and he groaned aloud, and answered:
'Ah, then it comes home to me — the old prophecy!
There was a seer here once, a great man and a good one,\nTelemus, Eurymus' son, who excelled in prophecy
and grew old prophesying among the Cyclopes.
He told me all this would come to pass in time:
that I would lose my sight at the hands of an Odysseus.
But I always watched for some big man, a handsome one,\nto come here, clothed in great strength;
and now a little man, a worthless thing, a weakling,\nhas put out my eye — after he crushed me with wine.
But come here, Odysseus —\nlet me set out a guest-gift for you,
and press the famous earth-shaker\nto give you passage home.
For I am his son, and he declares himself my father.
He himself, if he wills it, will heal me — and no one else,\nnone of the blessed gods, and no mortal man.'
So he spoke; and I answered him and said:
'Would to god I could strip you of breath and\nlife and send you down to the house of Hades
as surely as not even the\nearth-shaker will ever heal that eye.'
So I spoke; and he then prayed to the lord Poseidon,\nstretching out his hands to the starry heaven:
'Hear me, Poseidon who hold the earth, dark-haired one:
if I am truly yours, and you declare yourself my father,
grant that Odysseus, sacker of cities, never come home —\nthe son of Laertes, who has his home in Ithaca.
But if it is his portion to see his own people,\nto reach his well-built house and his own fatherland,
late may he come, and in evil case, all companions lost,
on another man's ship — and find trouble in his house.'
So he spoke in prayer, and the dark-haired god heard him.
Then once again he lifted a stone — far bigger —
whirled it, and let it fly, putting\nhis measureless strength behind it,
and brought it down just astern of the dark-blue ship —\nbarely — it missed the tip of the steering-oar;
and the sea heaved up under the falling rock,
and the wave carried her forward,\nand drove her toward the far shore.
But when we came back to the island where the other
well-benched ships waited all\ntogether, with the companions
sitting round them weeping, watching for us without end,\nthere we ran the ship up on the sands
and stepped out ourselves onto the surf-line of the sea.
And taking the Cyclops' flocks out of the hollow ship
we divided all, so that no man\nmight go cheated of his share by me.
But the great ram — my strong-greaved companions gave him
to me alone, when the flocks were shared,\na gift apart; and on the shore
I offered him to Zeus of the\nblack cloud, the son of Cronos,
lord of all, and burned the thigh-cuts.\nBut he took no heed of my offering:
he was pondering, even then, how all my well-benched ships
might be destroyed, and all my trusted companions.
So then all day long till the setting of the sun we\nsat feasting on meat past counting and sweet wine;
and when the sun went down and the dusk came on,\nthen we lay down to sleep on the surf-line of the sea.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,\nthen I roused my companions and ordered them
to board in their turn and loose the stern-cables.
And they came aboard at once and\ntook their places at the oarlocks,
and sitting in order they struck\nthe gray salt water with their oars.
From there we sailed on further, grieved at heart,\nglad to be out of death, having lost our dear companions.
